stories.headline: Cowboys first-rounder Caleb Downs living up to the hype
stories.summary: Downs has exceeded expectations throughout the offseason as the safety heads toward his NFL debut against the Giants in Week 1.
stories.body:
FRISCO, Texas -- When the rookies put on their training camp skit in the Dallas Cowboys' final days in Oxnard, California, there was little doubt what role Caleb Downs would play.

From the time the Cowboys selected him in the first round to the final camp practice last week at The Star, Downs and defensive coordinator Christian Parker have been within arm's length of each other.

Parker walking him through different situations, teaching him different techniques before practice and during breaks. Downs listening and learning through it all.

So when Downs appeared for the skit in a Parker-like sweatsuit, a pair of Jordans and stylish glasses, then spoke about Jay-Z, everybody in the room knew who he was. Downs would only smirk, "It was cool."

Brian Schottenheimer liked it, too.

"The mannerisms were very good," the coach said. "Christian's one of those guys that he is wanting to be in games and wanting to be doing extra, and they spend a lot of time together. You can see them before practice, working together. I think that's important for any player, but certainly a young guy that has the high expectations of himself that Caleb does."

Downs will make his NFL debut in nine days when the Cowboys take on the New York Giants. It's a moment he knew would be coming for years, well before he starred at Alabama for one season, becoming the first true freshman to lead the Crimson Tide in tackles, and at Ohio State, where he was a two-time All-American and a winner of the Jim Thorpe Award as the country's best defensive back.

Since the Cowboys selected Downs at No. 11, trading up one spot with the Miami Dolphins to make sure they would get their priority player, Downs has done nothing but show he is ready.

"He's very willing," Parker said. "He's very curious."

The curiosity is the product of growing up with a father, Gary Downs, who had a six-year career as a running back with three teams, and a family steeped in the game. He mastered three different defenses in three years in college.

When Downs arrived in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, in the winter of 2023, he prepared so much early on that the coaches had to make sure he knew he could not play in the Tide's bowl game. At Ohio State, it took him weeks to learn Jim Knowles' scheme, and then last year under Matt Patricia, who brought a complex scheme developed under Bill Belichick with the New England Patriots, Downs picked up in weeks not only the responsibilities of his own position but what everybody else was supposed to do too.

"He's hungry for knowledge," secondary coach Ryan Smith said. "He wants to learn. He wants immediate feedback, whether it's in the meeting room or walking through or just working on his footwork. ... He's definitely urgent, and I appreciate that about him. That's what you get usually with guys who've been in the league for a while. For him coming in as a rookie, it's cool to see."

He is being asked to play the nickel spot in the defense but also working as a deep safety at times. In the nickel, he has been asked to cover receivers such as CeeDee Lamb and KaVontae Turpin. In the joint practices against the Los Angeles Rams and New Orleans Saints, he defended Puka Nacua and Chris Olave.

"Mike Tyson said success breeds confidence and confidence breeds success," Downs said. "So I feel like those two work together and when you win at things and you do good at things, it allows you to feel more confident. And then when you succeed, it just continues to grow from there."

Tyson also said everybody has a plan until they get hit. As a slot defender, Downs also carries serious run game responsibilities, and he has been tasked in practice with taking on lead blocks from guard Tyler Smith and tackle Tyler Guyton.

"That's one of the things when you run some of those things that we have where he's got to fit the gaps every once in a while, you're going to run into an unfavorable matchup," Schottenheimer said. "But it's no different than if you're a safety or a corner and a big back like [Baltimore's] Derrick Henry gets out in space. It's like, 'OK, this might hurt a little bit, but I got to get him down.'"

Defensive passing game coordinator Derrick Ansley used a modern-game description of Downs.

"What he is, he's a positionless player," Ansley said. "He can play most anything if you get a chance to teach it to him. He can learn it on the fly."

Coaches say he rarely makes the same mistake twice. He can recognize patterns and concepts quickly, yet as camp went on, he was one of the last defensive backs to record an interception.

His first came in his a camp practice in front of Cowboys fans at Ford Center at The Star on Aug. 25.

Guarding Ryan Flournoy in tight red zone work, Downs was able to close the space and come down with the Dak Prescott pass in the back of the end zone. In an instant, he turned and punted the ball -- like other defenders had done in Oxnard -- in celebration.

To Schottenheimer, it wasn't done to mark that he finally had a takeaway.

"He knows there's a lot more to come, but he and Dak were having some good trash talk back and forth, which is good," Schottenheimer said. "And it was actually a little smirk on Dak's face when he saw it was Caleb that got the interception. I think he was excited -- not excited he threw an interception -- but that we're seeing the growth of what's going to be a really, really great player."

stories.headline: Mike Dean's 'games' claim is 'nonsense' - ex-Premier League ref Graham Scott
stories.summary: Former Premier League referee Graham Scott has accused Mike Dean of "clickbait" following the ex-referee's comments about "playing games" during top-flight matches.
stories.body:
Former Premier League referee Graham Scott has accused Mike Dean of "clickbait" following the ex-referee's comments about "playing games" during top-flight matches.

Dean revealed on Jamie Vardy's podcast this week that, during Premier League matches, he would play secret games that included seeing how long he could go for without giving a foul and his comments have caused considerable controversy.

"There used to be games we used to have, as a laugh we used to say 'Right, we'll kick off now, right. See how long we can go without blowing a whistle,'" Dean said on the podcast.

"I've done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR, obviously. Went 20-25 minutes without blowing a whistle -- 'Let it go, let it go, let it go.'"

Speaking to TalkSport, Scott -- who refereed in the Premier League between 2015 and 2025 -- said that what Dean had revealed about "playing games" was not true.

"I worked with Mike loads of times -- they're not true stories," Scott said. "I wish people wouldn't do this kind of thing. It's the audio equivalent of clickbait, isn't it?

"It's to try and get people interested and laughing. It's palpable nonsense. [...] I found him [Dean] quite shy, personally. I found him quite small when he was in a private situation.

"What happened on the field, what happened in referee meetings is he put on a persona that was way too far the other way, as a kind of coping mechanism."

- Mike Dean admits to playing secret 'game' to not blow whistle while refereeing Premier League matches

- Premier League's summer transfer market is dangerously out of control

- Ranked: Top 50 most expensive Premier League transfers this summer, by true cost

Scott added: "It is dispiriting. I'd challenge Mike, I'd say 'Okay, would you stand in front of the current refs and repeat all those things?' And of course he wouldn't, because they're not true."

Dean's former boss at Professional Game Match Officials Limited (PGMOL), Keith Hackett, insists the referee would not have been able to play the "games" he claims to have done while officiating.

Hackett said on X: "Mike Dean is in fantasy land!! The examination of performances assessors is forensic. When I was boss, referee's performances were forensically examined.

"Dean on my watch could not have done what he said with the monitoring systems in operation."

Hackett added he was "satisfied [Dean] is talking nonsense" and said: "He clearly has damaged his reputation. The fallout does not help current refs."

Pro Ref offered no comment about Dean's claims when approached by ESPN.

stories.headline: Taylor Harwood-Bellis left out of Aston Villa Champions League squad after expressing 'excitement' for 'biggest stage'
stories.summary: Taylor Harwood-Bellis was omitted from Aston Villa's squad for the Champions League, two days after arriving at the club and explaining his ambition to play in the tournament.
stories.body:
Taylor Harwood-Bellis was omitted from Aston Villa's squad for the Champions League, two days after arriving at the club and explaining his ambition to play in the tournament.

Harwood-Bellis signed for Villa on Tuesday, the Premier League's transfer deadline day, from Championship side Southampton.

He said upon arrival: "The club, in general, being such a prestigious Premier League club. And then you have the added bonus of the Champions League -- it doesn't fill me with anything but excitement.

"I can't get wait to get out there and show that I can hopefully do it on the biggest stage.

"We've seen the success that the club has had in Europe, winning the Europa League and going so far in the Champions League. I know that the club can relish in Europe as well."

However, that dream will be postponed until at least later this season because Villa's squad for the league phase of Europe's top competition did not include the defender.

If Unai Emery's side qualify from the league phase into the knockout stages they will submit a fresh squad which Harwood-Bellis could be added to.

stories.headline: How the US basketball system has shaped Nigeria's D'Tigress
stories.summary: The United States basketball system has played a major role in the development of Nigeria's national women's basketball team, known as D'Tigress.
stories.body:
The United States basketball system has played a major role in the development of Nigeria's national women's basketball team, known as D'Tigress.

Several players in Nigeria's FIBA Women's World Cup pool were born or developed in the USA, went through the NCAA system, or have connections to the WNBA.

Protland Fire's Amy Okonkwo began her college career at USC before transferring to TCU, where she became the Big 12 Sixth Player of the Year.

Ezinne Kalu played at Savannah State, finishing her career as the first player in program history to score more than 2,000 points.

Elizabeth Balogun's college career took her through Georgia Tech, Louisville and Duke. She was named ACC Freshman of the Year at Georgia Tech and reached the Elite Eight with Louisville before completing her college career at Duke.

Pallas Kunaiyi-Akpanah played four seasons at Northwestern, developing into one of the Big Ten's leading rebounders before spending time with the Chicago Sky.

Promise Amukamara played at Arizona State, while Enabosi starred at Delaware.

Head coach Rena Wakama has connections to both levels herself. She played college basketball at Western Carolina and is now an assistant with the Chicago Sky.

Those ties were evident during Nigeria's World Cup preparation, when D'Tigress played exhibitions against three WNBA teams, the Los Angeles Sparks, Minnesota Lynx and Indiana Fever, before continuing their preparations in China and Europe.

Ezinne Kalu
If there is a heartbeat to this D'Tigress team, it is Kalu. The 34-year-old point guard is the most experienced major-tournament player in Nigeria's current pool, having played at the 2018 World Cup, the Tokyo and Paris Olympics and four Women's AfroBaskets.

Kalu produced arguably the best basketball of her international career in Paris, averaging 18.5 points, four assists and three rebounds in four games.

She remains Nigeria's primary playmaker. At the World Cup qualifying tournament in March, Kalu averaged 9.4 points, 4.8 assists and 2.2 steals per game.

As the team head to Berlin, she is calling for Nigerians in Germany to give D'Tigress something approaching home support.

"We are heading to Berlin for the World Cup, and we need our people there to support us," Kalu said in an Instagram post.

"So we need every Nigerian near Berlin to come through. Bring your flag, your voice and energy."

Amy Okonkwo
Okonkwo has established herself as one of the best players, if not the best, in African basketball. The 6-foot-2 forward has won consecutive Women's AfroBasket MVP awards after leading Nigeria to the 2023 and 2025 championships.

The WNBA player averaged 14 points and six rebounds at the 2025 tournament and scored 19 points while playing all 40 minutes of the final against Mali.

Her ability to score inside, stretch defenses from the perimeter and rebound gives coach Rena Wakama one of her most versatile offensive options.

Berlin will be Okonkwo's World Cup debut, but hardly her first experience at this level. She played at both the Tokyo and Paris Olympics and has been a central figure in Nigeria's last two AfroBasket championships.

At club level, she has traversed Europe, and has also held her own with short but remarkable stints in the WNBA with Dallas Wings, Atlanta Dream and currently Portland.

Victoria Macaulay
The veteran center, who was born in New York, was arguably Nigeria's best performer during the March qualifying tournament. She averaged a team-leading 13.6 points and produced a team-best 16.4 efficiency rating over five games.

The Temple grad brings considerable international experience despite never having played at a World Cup, having represented Nigeria at the Tokyo Olympics and at the 2019 and 2025 AfroBaskets.

Alongside Musa and Pallas Kunaiyi-Akpanah, she gives Nigeria size, experience and physicality in the frontcourt.

Elizabeth Balogun
Balogun could be one of Nigeria's most intriguing players in Berlin. The guard averaged 10.6 points during the qualifying tournament and then produced one of the standout performances of Nigeria's World Cup preparation, scoring 26 points in an 88-77 victory over China in August.

Like Okonkwo, Balogun will be making her World Cup debut despite already having significant global tournament experience. She represented Nigeria at both Tokyo and Paris and was part of the 2023 and 2025 AfroBasket championship teams.

Balogun has also added another American professional connection to the roster after signing a development-player contract with the New York Liberty.

stories.body:
Formula 1 action is back in full swing and next up on the calendar is Monza, also known as the "Temple of Speed."

McLaren's Lando Norris sealed back-to-back victories after winning the Dutch Grand Prix to kick off the second half of the season last time out.

Kimi Antonelli is leading the championship by 59 points and following behind is his teammate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton both in second.

The Italian youngster will be hit with a grid penalty at his home race for taking a new engine.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know about the Italian Grand Prix.

How to watch

Sky Sports has exclusive F1 rights again in 2026 in the U.K., with every session live on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Italian Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Autodromo Nazionale Monza

The "Temple of Speed" is known for its long straights and heavy braking zones, and is the fastest track in Formula 1 history by overall average lap speed.

It's another classic circuit that has been on the calendar since 1950, only missing one year of racing in 1980 due to upgrading the track infrastructure.

It has one of the best podiums in the world as the famous Ferrari-loving tifosi flood onto the track after the race is finished. It's always a sight to be seen, especially if you are a Ferrari driver or an Italian driver.

Italian Grand Prix

Circuit: Autodromo Nazionale Monza; Monza, Italy

Previous winners
2016: Nico Rosberg, Mercedes

2017: Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes

2018: Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes

2019: Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

2020: Pierre Gasly, AlphaTauri

2021: Daniel Ricciardo, McLaren

2022: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

2023: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

2024: Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

2025: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

Other key stats

First F1 race: 1950

Lap record: 1:18.792, Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Laps: 53 laps of 5.8km. Total distance 306km

Most poles: Lewis Hamilton has seven at this circuit (2009, 2012, 2014-2017, 2020). Other pole sitters from the grid are Fernando Alonso (2007, 2010), Charles Leclerc (2019, 2022), Max Verstappen (2021 and 2025), Carlos Sainz (2023) and Lando Norris (2024).

Most wins: Lewis Hamilton (2012, 2014-2015, 2017-2018) and Michael Schumacher (1996, 1998, 2000, 2003, 2006) are tied on five wins each. Other winners from the current grid are Fernando Alonso (2007, 2010), Pierre Gasly (2020), Charles Leclerc (2019, 2024) and Max Verstappen (2022, 2023 and 2025).

Weather forecast

The weather for the Italian Grand Prix is forecast to be sunny all weekend with light winds, with highs of 32°C on Sunday.

What happened last year?

Max Verstappen set the pace with the fastest lap in F1 history after getting pole position in Monza.

The Dutchman set a time of 1:18.792 breaking Hamilton's record from 2020.

It was McLaren's Norris who was on provisional pole before Verstappen beat him to the line in the closing stages.

Verstappen then went on to win the race in commanding fashion, but there were some team orders taking place at McLaren.

Norris was running in second for the majority of the race, but after a slow pit-stop, the team asked Oscar Piastri to move aside and let him teammate back through for second place.

At the time, Piastri was leading the championship from Norris by 31 points.

Who will win this year?

The biggest news entering the weekend will be Antonelli's engine penalty that will hamper his opportunity to score maximum points during the race.

He leads the championship after winning six races, but title fights can change quickly, as we saw during the backend of the 2025 season.

McLaren's upgrades have certainly been working, but team boss Andrea Stella said that Monza will be the true benchmark in terms of its performance and progress.

Ferrari will be hungry to get a home win with either of its drivers, but Monza will typically suit those strong in straight line speed and high-speed corners, such as Mercedes.

Monza could be one of the best opportunities to close the gap in the title race and take advantage of Antonelli not being a threat at the front of the pack.

stories.headline: What we learned: Pressure can win Hawks the flag; the massive warning sign for Freo
stories.summary: The Hawks' outstanding pressure can win them a premiership, but the Dockers have a big problem after a 'morale-sapping' home qualifying final loss. Here's three things we learned from Hawthorn's win over Fremantle.
stories.body:
Hawthorn produced a stunning performance Thursday evening at Optus Stadium to upset minor premier Fremantle and advance to a second successive preliminary final.

Sam Mitchell's side will now enjoy the week off before returning to the MCG to hunt a place in the 2026 AFL Grand Final. Meanwhile, the Dockers will face the winner of Geelong and Carlton next week in a must-win semifinal.

Here are three things we learned from the game:

Hawthorn's relentless pressure can win the flag
It was a masterclass of pressure and intensity from the Hawks on Thursday evening in the west as they put the Dockers to the sword on their home deck to book their ticket to the final four once again.

The Hawks played the wet-dry conditions perfectly and completely stymied the minor premiers for four quarters. Sam Mitchell's side brought the heat from the opening siren, pressing up and hunting in packs, while never allowing their opponents a moment to breathe and settle into the contest.

They locked the ball inside their attacking forward 50 and had Fremantle's back six under siege for most of the evening, forcing the Dockers into 32 defensive half turnovers -- their most in a game all year. Neither the Docker defense, nor the midfield group, had any answers to stop the onslaught as they again buckled under the finals spotlight.

Mabior Chol set the standard in the opening minutes with two gut-busting efforts inside forward 50. His fleet-footed brigade of small forwards never stood still for a second, while co-captain Jai Newcombe and Dylan Moore were in-and-under all night long, combining for 14 tackles.

It was this insatiable intent and appetite for the contest that allowed Hawthorn to pile on six consecutive goals following Luke Jackson's early opener. The Hawks took a 33-point advantage into the main break, restricting Fremantle to that lone Jackson major. The margin remained the same at the final change and could only be cut to 32 by the final siren.

Thursday's performance was proof the stat sheet can sometimes be a tad misleading. The Dockers dominated total disposals (+74) and enjoyed an advantage in inside 50s (+6), while the clearance and contested possession counts were virtually identical. And yet this game only ever looked like having one victor.

Hawthorn will now enjoy a well-earned week off before returning to the MCG for a preliminary final. The three most likely opponents for that game all reside outside Victoria. If the home crowd support can be paired with the ferocity displayed against Fremantle, there's no reason they can't jag two more wins in 2026.

We should be seriously worried about these Dockers
Fremantle had been the team of the season. Minor premiers with 19 wins and four losses. An even more imposing record at Optus Stadium where they were unbeaten in 12 games, including a sensational come-from-behind win against these Hawks back in Round 9.

Unfortunately for Justin Longmuir and the legion of fans decked head to toe in purple, the Dockers waited until September to turn in their biggest stinker of the year. The Hawks played this game like the final it was and the all-conquering home side never appeared close to being up for the occasion.

Aside from All-Australian running defender Jordan Clark and the reliable Andrew Brayshaw, Fremantle had few winners on the night. Midfielders Shai Bolton and Caleb Serong were well below their best, Murphy Reid left his kicking boots at home, while forward pair Josh Treacy and Jye Amiss were just about unsighted throughout.

Thursday evening was Fremantle's lowest score of the season (40), while the 17 points scored from turnover were the fewest they had managed in a game since 2019 (excluding season 2020 which featured shortened quarters). It was also the club's second-worst game of the year for converting scores from inside 50s.

Fremantle will now have to pick themselves up, dust themselves off, and regroup for a do-or-die semifinal against either Geelong or Carlton next weekend. And while they'll likely be favoured to win that game, would anyone be tipping them with a high degree of confidence?

The loss to the Hawks is as morale-sapping as it gets. Not only because it undoes so much of the great work that was done throughout the year. Not because for them to lift the premiership they'd have to win three straight games, including two on the other side of the country. But because this club, and its supporter base, was adamant it had turned the corner following last year's disappointing home elimination final defeat to Gold Coast.

That one-point loss to end last year's campaign could prove costly 12 months on. All of a sudden the Dockers have lost two finals in a row on their home deck and will be sweating at the prospect of it becoming three in a row next weekend. Meanwhile, what would the Cats or Blues really have to lose?

If you don't want James Sicily at his worst, you don't deserve him at his best
Sure, at times he can play the role of the ultimate villain, but Hawthorn co-captain James Sicily can also be the coolest head you're likely to find behind the ball and one of the greatest assets in football come September.

On Thursday evening he was very much the latter. Sicily was simply sensational against the Dockers, leading the defensive group that completely nullified Fremantle's dangerous three-pronged attack.

Time and time again Sicily out-positioned and out-bodied the Fremantle forwards, drawing on all of his experience and smarts to put on a defensive clinic. He was always in the right place at the right time, always a step ahead of his opponent, and always composed with Sherrin in hand.

Sicily finished his night in the west with a team-high 26 disposals, a game-high 12 intercept possessions, 10 marks, and seven score involvements -- more than any player wearing brown and gold not named Nick Watson.

"We wanted to commit to being tough and taking the game on," Sicily told Fox Sports after the win. "The way we were in sync tonight is just going to give us so much confidence."

There's more than a few Hawks that can make claims to being their club's most important player, but it's hard to look past Sicily when he's in this type of form.

stories.headline: Matías Galarza joins Inter Miami from River Plate
stories.summary: Matías Galarza has joined Inter Miami CF from Argentinian side River Plate.
stories.body:
Matías Galarza officially joined Inter Miami CF from Argentinian side River Plate on Thursday.

The Paraguay midfielder signed a contract with Inter Miami on Wednesday night, officially securing Galarza's move to South Florida on the final day of the MLS transfer window.

Galarza is familiar with MLS have completed a season on loan with Atlanta United FC earlier this year. He recorded one assist in 13 appearances for Atlanta across all competitions -- including MLS regular season games and U.S. Open Cup play.

Galarza also played an integral role for Paraguay at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, scoring one goal in a group stage match against Türkiye and an assist in a shocking round of 32 win over Germany.

Galarza becomes Inter Miami's second signing on deadline day, joining Brazilian winger Riquelme Fillipi, whose deal was confirmed earlier on Wednesday.

The two players join the club as new head coach Cristian Gonzalez takes over for interim manager Guillermo Hoyos.

Inter Miami made several roster moves during this window, with a source confirming to ESPN that defender Noah Allen is set to join the Chicago Fire FC. The two clubs are in advanced negotiations, with a deal set to be finalized shortly.

The MLS secondary transfer window closed at midnight on Wednesday.

Allen was absent from Inter Miami training on Wednesday morning.

Inter Miami also loaned midfielder David Ruiz to the New York Red Bulls, with the Herons receiving $75,000 in 2027 general allocation money for the deal. The Red Bulls also hold the option to make Ruiz's move permanent at the end of the current season.

Inter Miami sits in second place on the Eastern Conference table with 42 points in 22 games.

stories.headline: Winners and losers of Cale Makar's $163.2 million contract
stories.summary: The deal for Colorado's franchise defenseman set a new high benchmark for NHL players, with impacts around the league.
stories.body:
Cale Makar made NHL history last week, becoming the first player to earn $20 million annually in his blockbuster contract extension with the Colorado Avalanche.

His deal is worth $163.2 million over eight seasons. The 27-year-old defenseman's average annual value is $20.8 million against the salary cap. While many anticipated Makar would reset standards with his new contract, the fallout from his deal with Colorado will impact the rest of the NHL.

Some teams, players and trends will end up winners because of it. Others ... not so much.

Here are some winners and losers of the Makar contract.

Winner: Colorado Avalanche
Obviously.

GM Joe Sakic said recently that "you can't win without superstars." That's what you'd expect to hear from a guy who won Stanley Cups as a player on teams that featured Hall of Famers such as Peter Forsberg, Ray Bourque, Rob Blake and this guy Patrick Roy in goal; but also from the guy who built a roster around Makar and center Nathan MacKinnon that produced a Stanley Cup win in 2022.

There's an argument to be made that the Avalanche have the best players in the world at center and on defense and now have them both locked up through 2031. Every team in the league is trying to build a winner. No one has that kind of foundation on which to build.

Sakic was blessed with a star defenseman who wanted to go max term (eight years) from the start of negotiations. No "wait and see" contract. No trying to sync up the end of his deal with that of a family member on another NHL team (more on that in a moment). Cale Makar wanted to give Colorado nine whacks at the piñata while he's under contract.

We can tsk-tsk the Avalanche for not leveraging that commitment into a friendlier cap hit, but the reality is that both Makar and his camp fully understood the current market and the one that Makar could create as an unrestricted free agent next summer. There was no steep discount to be had here, nor should there have been the expectation of one.

There are legit concerns about aging curves and overall health for a player who logs the kind of ice time that Makar does. Teams go into contract talks all the time with that in the back of their throats. But the inherent greatness of Makar, and this window to win with him on the blue line, outweigh those worries.

His cap hit will be recontextualized, as they all eventually are. The NHL is going to have the revenue streams from new media rights deals and at least two new teams inflating the cap during Makar's contract term. As one player agent told me: "By the time this deal is over, there will be guys in the league making $30 million per season."

Loser: Bill Guerin
First off, much respect to the Minnesota GM for facing a barrage of questions during a recent local media tour -- at the Minnesota State Fair, no less! -- about the status of his contract negotiations with Quinn Hughes. We've come to expect that kind of candor from Guerin, as both an NHL executive and U.S. national team general manager, but it's still refreshing when so many of his colleagues get camera shy during high-stakes negotiations.

Guerin told WCCO's Chad Hartman that there's "no tension" with Hughes and his agent, Pat Brisson, but refused to traffic in hypotheticals. Dan Barreiro of KFAN told Guerin he "can't trade" Hughes due to how much the Wild gave the Vancouver Canucks for the defenseman; Guerin reiterated that "we don't want to lose him and our fans don't want to lose him."

Hughes has one more season left at $7.85 million before becoming an unrestricted free agent next summer, and he's eligible to sign an extension now. If he signs before Sept. 15, he can max out at an eight-year term. If he signs as a free agent next summer, the max is six years -- although the max contract he could sign (20% of a projected $113.5 million cap in 2027-28) would be higher, at $22.7 million.

It's hard to find many around the NHL who believe Hughes will sign a long-term deal with the Wild. Most expect it'll be a three-year term that walks him up to 2030 when his brother Jack Hughes of the New Jersey Devils is an unrestricted free agent. But what about the money?

As Guerin did radio hits about Hughes amid the butter sculptures and lumberjack shows at the fair, there was one common theme: That Makar's deal impacts what Hughes could make on a new contract, but not dramatically.

"Could it affect you financially? Yeah. There's the bar with Cale Makar signing that contract in Colorado, but Quinn might be after different things. He's got different things in the life that's important to him," he told Hartman.

Guerin's theory: That Hughes has already made significant money in his career, so he can afford to make different types of decisions on his next contract. His current contract, signed in 2021, is worth $47.1 million.

"It doesn't have to be that 'Makar signed for this so he's got to sign for that.' No. He can do whatever the hell he wants because he's not going broke tomorrow," Guerin told KFAN.

Of course, Makar will have made $54 million on his current deal before starting on a $163 million contract in 2027-28.

It's possible that Guerin would have to overcompensate Hughes regardless of what Makar makes, like he did to keep Kirill Kaprizov in Minnesota. Makar's deal doesn't dramatically change the math on Hughes. It also doesn't uncomplicate what's already an extremely complicated negotiation for Guerin.

Winner: Matthew Schaefer
After just one season with the New York Islanders -- in which he was the unanimous choice for NHL rookie of the year -- Schaefer might already be in blank check territory for his next contract. The defenseman, who turns 19 this week, has that rare franchise-altering alchemy of on-ice ability and off-ice charisma that's been previously exhibited by players like Alex Ovechkin. He's that special.

And soon he'll be very, very rich.

Schaefer can sign an extension next summer as he enters the last year of his rookie contract. Islanders GM Mathieu Darche now has two contractual magnets pulling up Schaefer's salary: Makar, resetting the bar for defensemen at $20.4 million AAV; and San Jose Sharks phenom Macklin Celebrini, another transformative young player who will earn $18.8 million annually over five seasons.

Loser: Columbus Blue Jackets
The current holy trinity of NHL defensemen is Makar, Hughes and Zach Werenski, the latter of whom won the Norris Trophy last season ... and then blocked a trade to the Dallas Stars after communicating that he didn't plan on signing an extension with the Blue Jackets.

Werenski, 29, has since emphasized that he wants to remain in Columbus as long as the Blue Jackets are a playoff team that's trending in the right direction.

He's eligible to sign an extension next summer, with two years remaining on a deal that carries a $9,583,334 average annual value. The ceiling for Werenski as a 2028 free agent would be an AAV of $24.6 million. Whether or not his heart's still in Columbus could be a separate issue from whether the Blue Jackets would commit that kind of money for any player -- let alone a defenseman who will be in his early 30s by then.

Winner: Montreal Canadiens
Lane Hutson finished one point behind Cale Makar in scoring among defensemen last season. In 2027-28, when he's 23 years old, Hutson will count $11.55 million less against the salary cap than Makar does.

There are mitigating circumstances for Montreal's deal with Hutson, which he signed last October in the final season of his rookie contract. The defenseman was a 10.2(c) restricted free agent, leaving him with little leverage as a player ineligible for either an offer sheet or arbitration. But Montreal used that advantage to squeeze an eight-year deal with an $8.85 million annual cap hit out of Hutson.

It was praised as a bargain at the time -- many felt he'd at least hit $10 million AAV -- but given how the ground shifted after Makar's deal for scoring defensemen, it's an absolute steal.

This is going to be for Montreal like MacKinnon's second contract was for Colorado (seven years at $6.3 million annually): an epic underpayment of an elite player that allows his team to get a ton of other business done. Keep in mind the Avalanche won the Stanley Cup in Year 6 of that deal.

Loser: Analytics truthers
Cale Makar has been a Norris Trophy finalist in six of his seven NHL seasons, winning it twice and finishing second in the voting twice as well. He has a Calder Trophy and a Conn Smythe to his credit. He's considered the best defenseman of his generation, perhaps even the best player of his generation. Comparisons to Bobby Orr aren't met with a scoff but with respectful contemplation.

But there's another assessment of Makar -- in the present and for the duration of his contract -- that's worth considering: The one from analytics-driven skeptics who see Makar's deified status as more than a little bit owed to the greatness of MacKinnon.

Corey Sznajder had a nuanced look at this theory on All Three Zones, which included these numbers from Natural Stat Trick:

"Over the past three seasons, Makar has shared the ice with MacKinnon for 2,572 minutes compared to 1,434 minutes without him (all 5v5 by the way). In those minutes, the Avs own 58.1% of the shot attempts, 57.4% of the expected goals and 61.3% of the goals. In the minutes with Makar without MacKinnon the ice, Colorado owns only 47.3% of the shots, 48% of the expected goals and 52.2% of the goals. MacKinnon without Makar on the ice is at 56.6%, 55.7% and 66.8% in all three of those stats respectively," Sznajder wrote.

Those kinds of stats don't necessarily paint their on-ice partnership as symbiotic, but rather MacKinnon being the one driving the bus, while Makar stands over his shoulder like Keanu with Sandra Bullock in "Speed."

Obviously, the Avalanche don't care about any of this after giving Makar a record-breaking contract. He and MacKinnon are going to share the ice for Colorado until 2031 at a minimum. But this conjecture will continue to simmer in awards debates, player comparisons on social media and now in evaluating Makar under this megadeal.

Winner: player empowerment
As I wrote in June, the age of player empowerment is at hand for the NHL. We saw it in Brady Tkachuk leveraging a trade to his brother's team in South Florida, or in Dylan Larkin trying to force his way out of a long-term commitment to the Detroit Red Wings. But we also saw it in some of the mega-contracts that we signed in the offseason, with Makar's deal as the current apex.

Young stars like Celebrini ($18.8 million AAV) and Chicago's Connor Bedard ($15 million AAV) scored big in re-signing with their teams. Leo Carlsson shocked the NHL by signing a five-year, $18 million AAV offer sheet with the Philadelphia Flyers that the Anaheim Ducks matched.

(My favorite theory of the offseason, offered up by one NHL player agent: That Flyers ownership greenlit the Carlsson offer sheet as the ultimate long-term vengeance in the Cutter Gauthier drama with Anaheim. "They probably want to say, 'Hey, Philly's a good spot to be in. Don't [mess] with us.'")

There are always going to be players who take a "team-friendly" deal because the circumstances warrant it, like Connor McDavid earning less annually than Leon Draisaitl. But the ones breaking the bank are no longer the outliers, and they're going to keep breaking it. Some NHL teams are projecting the salary cap could rise to $150-$160 million by the 2031-32 season. Makar is just the beginning.

(Although, technically, Makar did just sign a team-friendly deal: $400,000 annually under the max, and one year before unrestricted free agency could have upped his ask to over $22 million annually.)

Loser: Short-term deals
Perhaps the most shocking aspect of Makar's extension wasn't the money but the term.

One hallmark of the NHL's player empowerment trend has been contract duration. Auston Matthews was one of the first huge names to go short-term, signing a five-year deal with the Toronto Maple Leafs in 2019 and then a four-year extension in 2023. Since then, Celebrini, Bedard, Carlsson and Nico Hischier of the New Jersey Devils have all signed five-year extensions, while defenseman Evan Bouchard went four years with the Edmonton Oilers.

But Makar's focus from the start of talks with the Avalanche was an eight-year term, an option that will not exist when the new CBA kicks in later this month.

"I think it gives us a lot of clarity in the sense of the direction we want to go in, hopefully being able to succeed in the next nine years, and have that stability in knowing that the contract is there and we have the pieces that we can build around," he said, via NHL.com.

Again, not everyone in the NHL can look around their locker room and see Nathan MacKinnon, with the proof of concept of having already won a Stanley Cup with him. Makar didn't have to take the "wait and see" deal that others in his tax bracket have with teams striving to become contenders. Makar knows what he has around him. And now, the Avalanche know they have Makar for the next decade.

stories.headline: NRL: Benji Marshall eyeing Tyson Frizell as Tigers seek to bolster pack
stories.summary: Wests Tigers have emerged as a potential landing spot for veteran Newcastle forward Tyson Frizell, with the club interested in bringing the former NSW and Australia representative to Concord next season.
stories.body:
Wests Tigers have emerged as a potential landing spot for veteran Newcastle forward Tyson Frizell, with the club interested in bringing the former NSW and Australia representative to Concord next season.

ESPN understands the Tigers have identified Frizell as a recruitment target as they continue to shape their roster for 2027.

Frizell, 34, is off contract at the end of the season and remains without a deal for next year as Newcastle turns its attention towards its finals campaign.

The experienced back-rower would add another hardened presence to a Tigers forward pack that has increasingly been built around a younger core.

Fonua Pole and Samuela Fainu have established themselves as key members of Benji Marshall's pack, while former Newcastle forward Kai Pearce-Paul joined the club this season and has added another long-term option on an edge.

Frizell would bring more than 300 games of NRL experience across Cronulla, St George Illawarra and Newcastle, along with an extensive representative resume for NSW and Australia.

Despite being in the latter stages of his career, Frizell has remained a reliable presence for Newcastle this season and continues to play significant minutes on an edge.

That experience would provide another senior presence for a Tigers roster preparing to undergo further change in 2027.

Jarome Luai will depart Concord at the end of the season to join Parramatta, leaving the Tigers without one of the most experienced members of their spine and leadership group.

The club has also fallen short of a long-awaited return to finals football this season, extending a drought that dates back to 2011.

The Tigers have already begun adding experience to their roster for next year, with Jayden Brailey set to arrive from Canberra, as exclusively reported by ESPN in July, while the club continues to survey the market in a bid to strengthen Marshall's squad.

Frizell has spent the past six seasons in Newcastle after joining the Knights from the Dragons ahead of the 2021 season.

For now, the veteran's immediate focus remains on Newcastle's finals campaign as the Knights prepare for their first game of the postseason.

stories.headline: Why Bucs' Mayfield has 'extra motivation' heading into season
stories.summary: The self-imposed deadline has passed for Tampa Bay's quarterback as he now turns his attention to the season.
stories.body:
TAMPA, Fla. -- When it comes to playing with a chip on his shoulder and betting on himself, Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield isn't kidding when he says, "That's something I'm pretty familiar with."

Throughout his career, Mayfield has shown both a willingness to fight and prove doubters wrong, but also that his tolerance for what he perceives as disrespect does have its limits. Are the Bucs testing them by having him play out the final year of his deal? Or will they get the most out of a player who "wants his lick back" in 2026?

He didn't get the contract extension he wanted by his self-imposed training camp deadline this summer and sources say there haven't been any talks since the Bucs' last offer on July 30.

Mayfield said once his deadline expired that he didn't want to have further discussions until the offseason, and he told his agent, Tom Mills, not to bother him unless he's "actually recognized" for his value.

The Bucs have been vocal about not wanting Mayfield to leave, with general manager Jason Licht saying last week during a preseason game broadcast, "I'm very optimistic about it."

"He wants to play," Licht said. "He wants to prove to us that he is the franchise quarterback that we said that he was.

"So, we'll just have to see how it plays out. I'll never close the door on anything in the short term, but right now, he's focused on football."

And then perhaps revealing the volatile nature of these situations, Licht gave a more measured response four days later.

"Well, we certainly respect him wanting to focus on the season," Licht said. "We're focused on the season. I've been here long enough [over 12 years] to know that in this league, I don't want to make predictions on what could happen, what will happen, what won't happen."

Despite the distractions that may come with all of this, Mayfield's teammates have had his back.

"I expect Baker to be Baker, and I expect him to lead us like he always does and I expect him to bring the best out of us," left tackle Tristan Wirfs said. "I think he's gonna play with his hair on fire."

STRAIGHT FROM LUBBOCK, Texas -- following Texas Tech's 41-16 season finale loss to Texas in 2013 -- Mayfield drove his Chevy Tahoe to Austin, right up to the back door of his Lake Travis High School football coach Hank Carter's home for a surprise visit.

Moments before, Carter had been on the phone with a coaching pal at Texas Tech -- where Mayfield had become the first-ever true freshman walk-on quarterback to start a season opener for a BCS school -- and told him, "Hey man, y'all are screwing this up. Why hasn't he been put on scholarship yet?"

Speaking to ESPN, Carter recounted the moment when Mayfield took a seat in his office at his home that day. Not only had Mayfield started seven games for the Red Raiders and accounted for 15 touchdowns and not been put on scholarship, but he was informed that they did not have one available for him that spring and couldn't give him one until something opened up.

And he was informed that coach Kliff Kingsbury was opening up the quarterback job for competition, which didn't sit well.

Carter asked, "Well, what do you think you're going to do?"

Carter said Mayfield responded, "'What am I going to do?' He goes, "I've got all my s--- packed in my car right now. I'm out. I already left."

Carter's response? "Oh my God."

Mayfield delivered the news to Kingsbury on Dec. 10. The following day, when it was announced that he'd won the Big 12 Freshman Offensive Player of the Year award, he made his departure public.

Mayfield and Carter picked up the conversation a few days later. Carter offered to help him find another school. But Mayfield had already made up his mind.

"I think I'm going to go to [Oklahoma]," Mayfield said.

He publicly declared his intentions to enroll there on Dec. 19, and on Jan. 3, the Sooners defeated Alabama in the Sugar Bowl, 45-31, with freshman Trevor Knight at quarterback.

"I go, 'Bake, this quarterback just hung 40 points on Nick Saban,"' Carter said. "I was like, 'Are you sure?'"

Mayfield told him, "Coach, I know that guy. He's a great guy," Carter said. "But then he said, 'I'll beat him out. I'll beat him out. I've wanted to go there my whole life. That's always been the school we rooted for.'

"He was just like, 'Screw it, I'm going,'" Carter said. "And I did not think that was the best decision, but I was wrong. He obviously knew exactly what he was doing. ... And yeah, the rest is history."

A Heisman Trophy, first-overall selection in the 2018 draft and three playoff appearances later, Mayfield finds himself in a situation to prove himself once again with the Bucs, who did not meet his July 28 deadline for a new contract. Instead, he'll play out the remainder of his contract, which ends after the season, and let the chips fall where they may in the offseason.

According to Mayfield, "Sometimes you have to put yourself backed into a corner and fight your way out."

And that's where he stands heading into the season with the Bucs, hoping to lead Tampa back into the playoffs after falling short last year.

"His mentality is that underdog mentality he's had since I'm sure he was 8 years old starting to play football," Tampa Bay offensive coordinator Zac Robinson said. "That'll never leave that guy, and it's a good thing.

"He believes in himself. Whether other people believe in him too, he really doesn't care."

MAYFIELD ASSEMBLED THE team before the Bucs' first camp practice and briefed them on his contract situation, emphasizing that it would not be a distraction and his focus was strictly on them and football. His teammates said the message was heartfelt and well-received.

"I'd say just how committed he is," right guard Cody Mauch said. "I mean, he set a deadline. He said his deadline's the beginning of training camp and he's sticking to it. And now he's like, 'I promise I'm all about ball.'

"It sucks to see him go through this and whatnot, but it's not going to change his mentality, the way he plays. I mean, he's going to go ball out and it's going to get made right."

Wide receiver Tez Johnson said Mayfield has been "true to his word" and "we trust him and we love him."

"When he said it's all ball for us, it was strictly all ball," Johnson said. "He's so eager to just go out there and just prove to the world that he belongs, and he deserves to be in that talk with the quarterbacks."

Nose tackle Vita Vea who had his own contract dispute that was ultimately resolved with a new deal on Aug. 19, empathized with Mayfield's frustration. While Vea was holding in -- attending practices but not participating -- Mayfield used his media availability to not only express frustrations about his own deal but to advocate for Vea's re-signing.

"Baker is the heart and soul of this team," Vea said. "You see the energy he brings on game day. We feed off of that too, not only the offense.

"I hope things get figured out with him. I know we'd all love to have him. Everybody loves Baker. That's somebody that you wish to have on your side on game day."

Mayfield spent the summer working to master Robinson's offense -- his fourth in four seasons in Tampa, although it has strong similarities to the one he operated under Liam Coen in 2024. He's also worked on some of the issues he felt he fell short in last year, like his rhythm and needing to tighten up his footwork.

"If you're out of rhythm in this system -- whether it's timing of the routes and the concepts -- bad things are going to happen," Mayfield said. "It starts with my feet and going through that and trusting the timing of that and going through the progressions, checking the ball down."

Quarterbacks coach Chandler Whitmer, who spent last season tutoring Heisman Trophy winner Fernando Mendoza en route to a national championship at Indiana, has been a stickler for footwork, to the point that Mayfield has joked that he wants to "put his little ass in a headlock and beat him up."

Mayfield then conceded, "But no, I like to be coached hard."

Licht, who has been on the opposite side of the table during those difficult contract talks, is seeing him demand even more of himself and believes he could possibly have the best year of his career.

"Shoot, he gets in here at probably 4 a.m," Licht said. "I can just see it. Not that he wasn't before, but I just see a bit extra motivation on his part."

LAST SEASON WAS an injury marred season -- not just for Mayfield, but for almost his entire cast of receivers, starting offensive line and running back Bucky Irving.

As a result, Mayfield wasn't as physically effective after an MVP-caliber start, but he scoffed at the notion that the team's hesitancy at a deal longer than two years stems from concern about his body holding up.

"I started every game last year ... the last three years," Mayfield said. "I don't know if that should ever be a question."

Mayfield's combined 51 starts over the last three years ties him with Jared Goff of the Detroit Lions and Josh Allen of the Buffalo Bills for the most quarterback starts in the regular season in that span. But he's taken 116 sacks (fourth most) in that span and been contacted 345 times (12th most).

"I think he's very mindful of that," Licht said. "I think all quarterbacks, as they progress through their career, I think they are a little bit more in tune with that."

Mayfield did admit on the "4th and South" podcast that he's intentionally taken hard hits to light a spark when making plays outside the pocket.

"Sometimes it might be first down, but our team's in a lull," Mayfield said. "There's certainly points I can definitely be better about it, and I know that. But every once in a while, the guys need a little kick in the ass."

The Glazers, who own the Buccaneers, have never had to sign off on top dollar quarterback money. They won their first Super Bowl with veteran journeyman Brad Johnson, who was not under a lucrative deal. Even when seven-time Super Bowl winner Tom Brady signed with the Buccaneers, he averaged $25 million per season. Twelve quarterbacks will make at least double that in 2026.

In their initial talks, Mayfield said the Bucs were "not anywhere close" to what he and his agent were looking for -- not to reset the market but to be in the range of his peers. Sources told ESPN's Jeremy Fowler, Mayfield and his agent used Green Bay's Jordan Love (four years, $55 million per year, $160.3 million total guaranteed), Jacksonville's Trevor Lawrence (five years, $55 million per year, $200 million total guaranteed), and San Francisco's Brock Purdy (five years, $53 million per year, $182.55 million total guaranteed) as comps during the negotiations.

Per a source with knowledge of the situation, Mayfield's issue wasn't just length of the deal or guaranteed money. While he did not set out to reset the market, $50 million per year would have put Mayfield 13th in the league among current deals.

But those numbers will jump significantly over the next eight to 12 months because several quarterbacks are in line for new deals in Lamar Jackson, C.J. Stroud, Caleb Williams, Drake Maye, Bo Nix and Jayden Daniels. The $50 million benchmark today will be $60 million soon, a source explained. Another not involved in Mayfield's negotiations but who represents one of those quarterbacks believes there will indeed be at least one $70 million quarterback. What also must be considered is that the salary cap is expected to rise.

Sources told Fowler that in the Bucs' last offer prior to camp, they did come in offering a two-year deal worth slightly above $100 million in total. But Mayfield wanted longer than that and he was dissatisfied with the guaranteed money.

When asked about ownership's comfort level in spending that kind of money long-term and the thought process in making that type of investment, Licht said, "You're always comfortable with a great player and you make things work."

Mayfield's also having to navigate the loss of his top wideout and the franchise's all-time leading scorer in Mike Evans, whose departure in free agency for the San Francisco 49ers sent shockwaves throughout the team.

Then he spent large portions of camp without three of his top four wide receivers in Jalen McMillan (knee sprain), Emeka Egbuka (toe sprain) and Johnson (groin strain). On top of that, Wirfs missed nearly all of camp with a hamstring strain but he returned to practice.

Wirfs returned to practice Aug. 19 and Johnson Aug. 25. On Wednesday, before the team broke for four days, McMillan and Egbuka were running off to the side with the training staff.

They all should be ready for the season, with Bowles saying "They're headed in the right direction," but Mayfield believes their absences gave them a chance to explore different packages and work on his rapport with rookie third-round draft pick Ted Hurst III, who the Bucs believe possesses a lot of the physical attributes as Evans.

"You can just see it in [Mayfield's] eyes every time he takes the field," Johnson said. "When he's in a huddle calling a play, he's very intentional with the young guys and just getting them to learn because it's a moving train."

Mayfield threw a jump ball to Hurst during a two-minute drill in joint practices at the New York Jets. While he didn't come down with it, Hurst told ESPN it "gave me a sense that he believes in me to attack the ball."

Which is where Mayfield is now, attacking his preparation for Week 1 at the Cincinnati Bengals on Sept. 13 (1 p.m. ET, FOX). He's aware that some prognosticators have expressed doubts about a team without Evans, and about his health, or how a looming contract situation could negatively impact his headspace -- never mind that he embraces the motivation.

"Baker's pissed off every year and every game," Bowles told WDAE Radio this week. "He wants to beat the piss out of somebody. This is nothing new. It's a normal deal for him, whether it was a contract or not. We'll get the best Baker Mayfield that you can probably get."

Carter added, "He loves that. I don't think he always did love it. Certainly growing up -- that's not something that feels great, but I think now he's a master at it. And so any type of adversity that comes his way, he's just going to be like, 'Okay, no problem. We're going to figure this out.' And that's what he does well."

Mauch believes Mayfield when he says, "It's only going to get worse from here."

"He's going to go off," Mauch said. "... No doubt in my mind, he's going to go up and [and put up MVP or Offensive Player of the Year numbers] and get even more money now. So it's going to work out better for him in the end. I'm excited to see the way Bake uses this year."

Carter's excited as well, because he knows firsthand what can come of doubting his former player.

"I mean, he's always had the mindset of, 'Yeah, I'm not going to let you get one over on me,' Carter said. "That's kind of his deal. I've been saying this about him for a long time. I believe in trends, so I know how it'll work out for Baker. It's going to work out good because it always does."

stories.headline: Liverpool sign Djylian N'Guessan, 18, for next season
stories.summary: Liverpool have signed teenage forward Djylian N'Guessan although he won't play for the club until at least next season.
stories.body:
Liverpool have signed teenage forward Djylian N'Guessan although he won't play for the club until at least next season.

The 18-year-old will sign for Liverpool on a permanent deal in January from Saint-Etienne, but will spend this campaign on loan at Stade Brestois.

After debuting in January 2025 for Saint-Etienne, the French forward played 13 times and scored once.

N'Guessan played seven times for France in the 2025 Under-20 World Cup. Last summer he was named in the Team of the Tournament at the U17 European Championship, having scored four goals for France.

Similarly, Liverpool also wrapped up the £30 million ($41m) signing of goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans who will spend this season away on loan.

Brughmans, also 18, has signed from Belgian side KRC Genk where he will remain on-loan for this campaign.

The Italy international is joined by Wataru Endo among those omitted by new boss Andoni Iraola.

Liverpool confirmed their squad ahead of the start of their European campaign against Atlético Madrid at Anfield on Sept. 9.

Both players will be unavailable for the league phase unless Liverpool are able to make a permitted change to their squad, normally injury related.

UEFA rules limit sides to a 25-player List A, with eight places reserved for 'locally trained' players, of which four must have been at the club for three seasons between the ages of 15 and 21.

Younger players can be registered separately on List B if they meet UEFA's age and development requirements, but Chiesa and Endo are not eligible.

The 28-year-old misses out with summer arrival Víctor Muñoz included, alongside Conor Bradley, who is continuing his rehabilitation from a knee injury in February. Giovanni Leoni, who suffered an ACL tear in September 2025, is also on the list.

Chiesa is currently out with a muscle injury, though a long-term absence is not expected.

Endo made only eight Premier League appearances in 2025-26, seven of them from the bench, while he featured just once in Liverpool's run to the Champions League quarterfinals.

- Lindop: Liverpool needed to add depth in the transfer window. They didn't get it

- Andoni Iraola: Bradley Barcola could make Liverpool debut against Ipswich

- Champions League draw: Good games for Liverpool, bad for Barcelona

The Reds will play eight fixtures at this stage of the competition, with home games against Atlético, Porto, Villarreal and Lens.

They will travel to face Austrian side LASK, Fenerbahce, Club Brugge and Inter Milan.

Liverpool have instead included injured forward Hugo Ekitike in their squad despite the Frenchman currently being sidelined.

As expected, Ekitike's compatriot Bradley Barcola is on the list after his move from Paris Saint-Germain, worth up to £123 million ($166 million).

stories.headline: Nigeria's D'Tigress at the 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup - Everything You Need to Know
stories.summary: Nigeria's D'Tigress head to the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup in Berlin as a team with an unusual combination of tournament experience and World Cup unfamiliarity.
stories.body:
Nigeria's D'Tigress head to the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup in Berlin as a team with an unusual combination of global tournament experience and World Cup unfamiliarity.

Nigeria arrive as five-time defending African champions and the No. 8-ranked team in the FIBA world rankings, looking to improve on their best World Cup finish, an eighth-place showing in 2018.

The expanded 16-team World Cup runs from September 4 through13, with Nigeria drawn in Group B alongside France, South Korea and Hungary.

Here is everything you need to know about D'Tigress in Berlin.

How they qualified
Nigeria booked their place in Berlin by winning the 2025 FIBA Women's AfroBasket in Abidjan, defeating Mali 78-64 in the final to claim a fifth consecutive continental championship.

No country had previously won five consecutive Women's AfroBasket titles, and Nigeria's victory extended an unbeaten run in the competition that dates to 2015. D'Tigress have now won 29 consecutive AfroBasket games.

Ezinne Kalu led Nigeria with 20 points in the final, while Portland fire's Amy Okonkwo scored 19 as D'Tigress recovered from a slow start to pull away in the second half.

Okonkwo, who averaged 14 points and six rebounds during the tournament, was named MVP for the second consecutive AfroBasket.

Nigeria subsequently competed at the World Cup qualifying tournament in Lyon-Villeurbanne in March despite already having secured qualification as African champions.

They finished 2-3, beating Colombia 70-37 and the Philippines 101-84, while losing to South Korea 77-60, France 93-86 and Germany 81-73.

Those results carry additional significance into Berlin. Two of the teams that beat Nigeria in France, South Korea and France, have been drawn in their World Cup group.

Previous World Cup appearances
For all their success in Africa, D'Tigress have relatively little World Cup history. Berlin will be only Nigeria's third appearance at the tournament, with their tournament debut coming 20 years ago in Brazil in 2006, when they lost all five games.

It took another 12 years for them to make their breakthrough. At the 2018 World Cup in Spain, D'Tigress beat Turkey 74-68 for their first victory at the competition. They followed that by beating Argentina before defeating Greece in the qualification game to become the first African team to reach the Women's World Cup quarterfinals.

Their run ended against eventual champions the United States, but their eighth-place finish remains Nigeria's best at a World Cup.

Nigeria qualified for the 2022 tournament in Australia but did not participate after the Nigerian government withdrew the country's basketball teams from international competition amid a long-running leadership dispute within the Nigeria Basketball Federation.

That means Berlin will mark D'Tigress' return to the World Cup for the first time in eight years.

African dominance to global contenders
Nigeria's status in international basketball has changed considerably since their 2018 World Cup run. D'Tigress have won every Women's AfroBasket they have entered since 2017, claiming championships in 2017, 2019, 2021, 2023 and 2025.

The biggest evidence that their dominance could translate beyond Africa came at the Paris Olympics, when they became the first African basketball team, men's or women's, to make the Olympic quarterfinals before losing to the juggernaut that is Team USA.

On the plus side, that run pushed them into the FIBA women's world top 10 for the first time and they enter Berlin ranked No. 8.

Sadly they failed to build on that when they were withdrawn from the very next Games, the 2022 tournament in Australia.

But they have come storming back and while a return to the World Cup quarterfinals would match the achievement of the 2018 team, going further would take D'Tigress into territory no African women's, or even men's team have previously reached.

The Rena Wakama effect
Nigeria's rise has become closely associated with Rena Wakama.

Wakama became the first female coach to win the Women's AfroBasket when she led Nigeria to the 2023 championship and followed it with another title in 2025.

Between those championships came Paris. Nigeria's aggressive defense became one of the stories of the Olympic tournament, with D'Tigress applying pressure across the floor, forcing turnovers and turning those mistakes into transition opportunities.

After winning her first AfroBasket in 2023, Wakama recalled the moment she realized how much resilience she had in the team.

"Against Mozambique, we were down by 10 or 12 points," she said. "I looked into their eyes, and they told me: 'Coach, we're not going to lose this game.' And they came back to win."

Wakama's preparation for Berlin has been unusual because she has had to combine the national-team job with her role as an assistant coach with the WNBA's Chicago Sky.

Earlier this year, Wakama said the qualifying tournament in France was part of a broader process of testing Nigeria against the level of opposition they will encounter at the World Cup.

"Our preparations have been intense, and this tournament here in Lyon is an important part of that process," Wakama said.

"It gives us the opportunity to test ourselves against strong competition and evaluate where we're as a team."

stories.headline: What makes Max Verstappen so good? Career, background and F1 records
stories.summary: Max Verstappen is returning to his racing roots and is facing 100 drivers in a unique event called Max vs. 100 where the Formula 1 star will attempt to overtake 100 challengers, starting from the back of the grid.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen is returning to his racing roots and is taking part in a unique event called Max vs 100 where the Formula 1 star will attempt to overtake 100 drivers, starting from the back of the grid.

The 28-year-old currently races in F1, the highest tier in motorsport. He is one of the fiercest competitors out there and is known for his aggressive driving style and fearless overtaking.

But if you have never heard of him, or want to learn more, here is everything you need to know.

- Max vs 100: F1 superstar Verstappen to race drivers in karting event - live on Disney+

Who is Max Verstappen?
Verstappen was born in Belgium to his Dutch father Jos and his Belgian mother Sophie. His father raced in F1 between 1994-2003 and had two podium finishes, while his mother competed in karts. He currently resides in Monaco.

Who does he race for?
Verstappen started racing go-karts when he was just four years old and started to compete in championships at seven.

He then made his way through the ranks winning several world and European titles in 2013. He raced just one season in Formula 3 before skipping Formula 2 and heading straight to Formula 1.

In 2015, he signed for Red Bull junior team Toro Rosso at the age of 17 before he was promoted to Red Bull a year later.

He then went on to become the youngest ever grand prix winner after taking victory at the Spanish Grand Prix and has been at Red Bull ever since, becoming the most successful driver at the team.

He signed a long-term contract back in March 2022 to stay at the Milton Keynes-based team until the end of 2028, and before the Dutch Grand Prix this year he penned a new deal keeping him at the team until 2030.

What has he achieved?
It was clear from the early days that Verstappen was going to be an exceptional racing driver and he's become a phenomenon since with a killer instinct.

He's had 244 race starts in F1 and has been on the top step of the podium 71 times. He's been on the podium 131 times and is just two pole positions away from reaching 50 career poles.

The Dutchman has four world championships which he won back-to-back in a dominant Red Bull era between 2021-2024.

He also has an impressive list of achievements to his name, one being in 2023 where he recorded the most wins [19] and the most podium finishes [21] in a single season. He also recorded 10 consecutive race victories.

When is Max vs 100?
The event is taking place on Sept. 16 and will be streamed live on Disney+.

Why is he racing in Max vs 100?

Verstappen has never been shy of getting his teeth stuck into other forms of motorsport away from Formula 1. He most recently made his debut at the iconic Nürburgring 24 Hours in May, driving a Mercedes-AMG GT3.

This will be a slightly different challenge for the Dutchman, but no doubt one he will enjoy with his competitive nature.

"In go-karts you learn all the basics: starts, defending, overtaking," Verstappen said. "Of course, I spent a long period of my life go-karting, so it's always nice to return."

The event is taking place at Silverstone in the U.K. and a circuit has been purpose-built for the occasion. It's set to be the biggest go-kart event in the world.

- Max Verstappen deal: Good news for Red Bull and F1, bad news for the driver market

- Max Verstappen ends F1 speculation by signing new Red Bull contract to 2030

How is his 2026 F1 season going?
The 2026 season is one with big regulation and rules changes and Red Bull are currently at the back of the front running teams, but are ahead of the midfield pack.

Verstappen is still searching for his first race win of the season, but has been on the podium four times.

He's currently sixth in the title championship and is 130 points adrift from title leader Kimi Antonelli.

stories.headline: Kawhi investigation fallout: How the Clippers' roster is affected
stories.summary: After being punished for cap circumvention in 2000, Minnesota went nearly two decades without any playoff success. Is the same in store for Steve Ballmer's franchise?
stories.body:
From a team-building perspective, the most ruinous element of the NBA's punishment of the LA Clippers for salary cap circumvention surrounding Kawhi Leonard is the loss of five first-round draft picks, one each in 2029, 2030, 2031, 2032 and 2033.

There is only one precedent for such a serious punishment in NBA history: when the league similarly revoked five first-round picks from the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2000 for salary cap circumvention. In that case, the Timberwolves had come to an illegal agreement with free agent big man Joe Smith. (Then-commissioner David Stern ultimately returned two of the first-round picks.)

Looking back at how Minnesota navigated -- and suffered from -- that forfeiture can help inform our understanding of how the Clippers might fare in the years to come, as they bear the brunt of the NBA's discipline.

Minnesota's precedent
For the Timberwolves, the turn of the millennium was a terrible time to suffer such a drastic punishment. They'd been the NBA's worst team for years after joining as an expansion franchise in 1989; for the first seven years of their existence, they never won more than 29 games in a season.

But in 1995, they drafted high schooler Kevin Garnett with the No. 5 pick, and their trajectory finally started to improve. The Timberwolves won 21 games in 1994-95, the season before Garnett was drafted, but steadily rose to 50 wins by 1999-00.

Then the hammer came down, and the Timberwolves lost their first-round picks from 2001 through 2005.

Their win totals soon stalled out. After winning 50 games in 1999-2000, the Timberwolves won 47, 50 and 51 games over the next three seasons -- strong records still, but no longer showing evidence of further progression.

Minnesota finally took a leap in the 2003-04 campaign, after offseason trades for Sam Cassell and Latrell Sprewell. The Timberwolves won 58 games and landed the West's No. 1 seed, and Garnett won MVP. Minnesota went on to reach the conference finals -- winning the franchise's first two playoff series in the process -- before falling to the Lakers in six games.

But that one superlative season proved to be the Timberwolves' high point as a franchise (at least until the 2020s). Minnesota dropped to 44 wins and missed the playoffs in 2004-05, then peeled off 12 consecutive losing seasons through 2017. Garnett was traded to Boston during that drought, and it took more than a decade to recover.

So, how did the Smith sanctions ultimately affect Minnesota? On the one hand, the team still reached the playoffs in each of the next four seasons after they were levied, culminating in a conference finals run.

But on the other hand, it's hard not to wonder how much more competitive the Timberwolves could have been atop the Western Conference, and how much longer their run could have lasted, had they been able to make first-round picks during those lost draft years. Losing all of those picks conceivably cost the Timberwolves a title.

Garnett was a 24-year-old just entering his prime in 2000, but Minnesota didn't have the resources to add more young talent around him. In 2003-04, it was the third-oldest team in the NBA, according to Basketball Reference. And from 2001 through 2005, only three Timberwolves age 25 or younger averaged double-digit points in a season: Garnett himself, Wally Szczerbiak (the No. 6 pick in 1999, before the Smith case) and Chauncey Billups, a free agent signing who'd leave for Detroit the following summer.

The Timberwolves ended up selecting seven players in the draft from 2001 through 2005: five second-rounders and two first-rounders. Only one of those seven players provided even modest production in Minnesota, and that was too little, too late for the Garnett era.

Why the Clippers' future could be better -- or much worse

The comparison between the Timberwolves in 2000 and the Clippers in 2026 isn't perfect, for reasons that could provide both optimism and deep pessimism for Clippers fans.

On the positive side, seeing how the Timberwolves continued reaching the playoffs, and even reached their first conference finals, despite the lack of draft picks should be encouraging. And while the Timberwolves were devoid of first-round picks for half a decade after their punishment -- until the NBA returned two of them -- the Clippers' cupboard isn't bare, especially if their trade of Leonard back to Toronto goes through, now that the NBA has completed its investigation.

They still have a first-round pick next summer. (The Thunder can swap first-round picks with the Clippers in 2027, but the Clippers can then swap with the Raptors, per the reported terms of the Leonard trade.) And even as the NBA takes away one pick from five consecutive drafts starting in 2029, the Clippers should still have picks in 2029, 2031 and 2033, due to holding extras from the Leonard and Ivica Zubac trades.

The Clippers also managed to add a prized prospect to their team just under the wire, when they selected Keaton Wagler with the No. 5 pick in June. And their future cap sheet looks squeaky clean, giving them the theoretical ability to make upgrades in free agency -- if any star player is willing to join a franchise that was so recently embroiled in scandal.

But there are also numerous disadvantages for the Clippers, even relative to what Minnesota experienced after the Smith punishment. Most notably, the Timberwolves were a 50-win team that revolved around a young future MVP at the time, and his brilliance is the main reason that Minnesota remained competitive in its years without picks.

Conversely, the Clippers are coming off a season in which they missed the playoffs, and they're in the process of trading their best player. While Darius Garland and Wagler are both full of potential, neither guard is likely to approach Garnett's individual heights.

Moreover, the Garnett-era Timberwolves' best season came after they landed Cassell -- who made the All-NBA second team in Minnesota -- and Sprewell in trades. But they didn't need to trade a single draft pick to acquire those veteran contributors.

That was a different time; now, almost every win-now trade involves draft picks headed the other way. Yet the Clippers can't make those deals for the foreseeable future. Even if they have a few picks from other teams, the Stepien rule forbids them from trading those selections.

In other words, the Clippers have no trade flexibility for the foreseeable future, even if they see potential avenues to improve their roster.

And while the Timberwolves' loss of draft picks started immediately -- the NBA's ruling came in 2000 and began with the 2001 draft -- the Clippers' won't kick in for another three years, which means it will extend even farther into the future. If there's light at the end of the tunnel, it's a long ways away.

It's possible that the NBA could mellow its harsh discipline over time and return some of the Clippers' picks. There is some precedent here, not only from the Timberwolves receiving this grace in the early 2000s, but also from the 1980s, when the NBA gave the Cleveland Cavaliers "bonus" draft selections in 1983, 1984, 1985 and 1986 after owner Ted Stepien had traded all of Cleveland's picks away.

But that's a dim silver lining, because at the moment, the Clippers' situation looks even more dire than the Timberwolves' did a quarter-century ago. Hopefully their fans enjoyed their team's trip to the conference finals in 2021 -- which Leonard infamously missed due to a knee injury -- because it could be a long, long time before the franchise is competitive enough to return.
